early_childhood_ed.summary: No new early childhood education or childcare statements were found from Rep. Harshbarger in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: Harshbarger's press coverage this week was dominated by two unrelated topics: her TRUTH in Coverage Act (requiring insurers to cover detransition-related care) and a letter pressing the American Medical Association for transparency on CPT billing code changes for neurostimulator devices, which she said could 'make having a baby MORE expensive' by raising childbirth-related costs (a tangential, cost-of-childbirth angle rather than a childcare/early-education policy). Separately, Tennessee enacted the Child Care Red Tape Reduction Act (effective this week) to streamline permitting for new child care centers, and a new SmartAsset study found Tennessee child care averages roughly $14,000/year, about 17% of family income; neither development was tied to public statements from Harshbarger in the reviewed period. Her most recent nutrition-related legislative activity remains the H.R.9389 nutrition education bill introduced in June 2026, prior to this window.

child_hunger.summary: No new SNAP, child hunger, or school meals statements were found from Rep. Harshbarger in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
child_hunger.details: Harshbarger did not appear in coverage of SNAP or child hunger issues this week. Background context for TN-1: about 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's tightened work requirements and eligibility rules, part of a national decline of roughly 4 million SNAP participants (about 10%) since the law took effect, with ProPublica estimating hundreds of thousands of affected recipients nationally are children. Tennessee's own SNAP soda/candy purchase restriction, originally set to begin July 31, 2026, was thrown into question this week after a federal court ruled against USDA's legal authority to approve the food-restriction waivers used by Tennessee and four other states. Harshbarger's most recent related legislative action is the nutrition education bill (H.R.9389) she introduced in June 2026, which predates this window and was not the subject of new coverage this week.

parental_support.summary: No new statements on paid leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare costs were found from Rep. Harshbarger in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: Harshbarger's week was dominated by the TRUTH in Coverage Act (detransition insurance coverage) and her AMA transparency letter on CPT billing codes, neither of which addresses paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare affordability directly, though her AMA letter did reference concerns that certain billing changes could raise the cost of childbirth. Tennessee context: a new SmartAsset (2026) cost-of-raising-a-child study ranked Memphis and Nashville among the two most affordable major U.S. metros overall (about $19,900 and $21,200/year respectively), but noted child care alone still consumes roughly 17-20% of a typical Tennessee family's income, an ongoing state-level affordability pressure that was not the subject of comment from Harshbarger this week.

Separately, Tennessee's Child Care Red Tape Reduction Act took effect this week to ease permitting for new child care centers statewide (a state-level, not Burchett-driven, policy), and at the federal level Senators Cassidy and Tuberville introduced the STOP Child Care Fraud Act targeting fraud in the Child Care and Development Block Grant program; Burchett was not reported as a co-sponsor or commenter on that Senate bill.

child_hunger.summary: Burchett, chairing the House DOGE subcommittee, demanded five years of SNAP beneficiary data from five Democratic governors this week and continued pressing SNAP fraud/integrity issues, following a June 25 hearing his panel held on 'Combating Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in SNAP.'
child_hunger.details: As chairman of the House Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency (DOGE), Burchett sent letters this week demanding SNAP disbursement data from the governors of New York, California, Illinois, Michigan, and Pennsylvania, all of whom have declined to comply with a USDA data-sharing request. Burchett argued non-compliance masks potential fraud, noting the USDA has already identified an estimated $3 billion annually in potential waste, fraud, and abuse from the 29 states that did share data (including roughly 186,000 deceased individuals still receiving benefits and over 500,000 people found registered in multiple states). New York Gov. Kathy Hochul's office denied wrongdoing and accused Republicans of using the fraud framing to justify cutting food assistance to vulnerable residents; the other four governors had not responded to Burchett as of this week. This follows a June 25, 2026 House Oversight Committee hearing (chaired by Burchett) titled 'Combating Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in SNAP,' where Republicans questioned food industry influence on SNAP nutrition rules and highlighted card-skimming and trafficking fraud; Burchett stated 'every SNAP dollar is intended to help feed eligible individuals in need... that's not where every dollar goes.' Separately, a Knox News opinion column published July 20 criticized Burchett for 'condemning waste' in SNAP and elsewhere while staying silent on Trump-administration spending (citing a roughly $600 million White House ballroom project), arguing his anti-waste focus is selectively applied. This activity occurs against a backdrop in which about 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (part of a national decline of roughly 4 million participants, nearly half of whom in some states are estimated to be children), and a federal court ruling this week blocked USDA's approval of Tennessee's planned SNAP soda/candy purchase restriction, which had been set to take effect July 31, 2026.

name: Anna Golladay
bio: Chattanooga progressive who previously ran for City Council. Announced February 2026.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Golladay named childcare costs among the district's most urgent affordability issues in her Knox News/USA Today voter guide interview (published July 16, 2026) and in a Chattanooga Times Free Press profile (July 13), though she did not detail a specific early-childhood-education policy proposal.
early_childhood_ed.details: In the Knox News U.S. House District 3 primary voter's guide (published July 16, 2026), Golladay, 52, described as a small business owner and community organizer, told Knox News: 'By far it's the affordability crisis. We have residents that I talk to every day who are concerned about the price of groceries and housing and gas and child care. Those things are not coming with an increase in wages, and that in and of itself is a challenge. We have folks that aren't able to make the numbers work because the numbers don't actually work.' In a companion Chattanooga Times Free Press piece (July 13-14), Golladay similarly named 'the cost of living -- food, shelter, childcare, healthcare and utilities' as the district's most urgent issues, which she said she would address by expanding low-income housing tax credits and funding community land trusts. This tracks with statewide reporting this week (Elizabethton Star, July 17) on Tennessee's new Child Care Red Tape Reduction Act and Nashville meeting only 56% of demand for children under 5, though Golladay was not directly quoted in that state-level story.

child_hunger.summary: Golladay pledged to increase federal spending on SNAP/WIC and to protect federal food aid programs, in on-record statements to the Chattanooga Times Free Press published July 13-14, 2026 as part of its TN-3 Democratic primary candidate guide.
child_hunger.details: In the Chattanooga Times Free Press's July 13-14, 2026 profile of the TN-3 Democratic primary (Golladay vs. Bryan Martin), Golladay stated directly: 'In addition to ensuring Social Security is fully funded, I would support increasing federal spending on SNAP/WIC, SUB benefits, the low income housing tax credit, community land trusts, the child tax credit, Title I/IDEA funding for public schools and Medicaid.' She separately said the district's most urgent issues include the cost of food and that she would fight in Congress to 'protect programs like federal food aid and funds for rural hospitals.' A Times Free Press opinion column endorsing Golladay (July 14) reinforced this profile, describing her as focused on making Tennessee's economy 'affordable for the average Tennessean' and citing her own financial strain after ACA subsidies expired as informing her advocacy for economic protections for working people. This SNAP/WIC pledge came the same week Civil Eats (July 16) and other outlets reported roughly 4 million Americans (and about 1 million children in states with available data) had been dropped from SNAP nationally since OBBBA took effect, with an estimated ~100,000 Tennesseans affected, and the same week Tennessee's SNAP soda/candy purchase ban was slated to take effect July 31 (pending litigation).

parental_support.summary: Golladay pledged to expand the Child Tax Credit and support for families as part of increased federal domestic spending, in the same July 13-14, 2026 Chattanooga Times Free Press candidate profile, alongside her broader push to raise the minimum wage and lift the Social Security payroll tax cap.
parental_support.details: In her July 13-14 Times Free Press candidate questionnaire response, Golladay explicitly listed 'the child tax credit' among the federal programs where she would support increased spending, alongside SNAP/WIC, the low-income housing tax credit, community land trusts, Title I/IDEA school funding, and Medicaid. On broader worker/family economics, she said: 'Thirty-six percent of Tennessee's workforce earns less than $15 an hour; the federal minimum wage has not been raised since 2009. I will fight to raise the federal minimum wage and tax the super-rich so they are paying their fair share,' and she pledged to 'immediately push for a lift of the payroll tax cap' to fund Social Security. Golladay also named childcare and healthcare costs directly among the district's top affordability concerns for families (see early childhood ed section) and, per the Times Free Press opinion endorsement (July 14), has personal experience with rising healthcare costs (she said her ACA premiums rose to $2,500/month after subsidies expired), which she cites as informing her family-affordability platform. No statement specifically on paid family leave was located this week.

name: Andy Ogles
bio: Two-term incumbent facing FEC violations and Ethics Committee scrutiny. Just $85K cash on hand (Q1 2026) — among the lowest of any U.S. House incumbent nationally. Trump-endorsed despite ongoing investigations.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No new early childhood education, pre-K, Head Start, or childcare statements from Andy Ogles were found in the July 14–20, 2026 window; Ogles's public messaging this week focused almost entirely on immigration and his 'Anchors Away Act.'

This occurred the same week Tennessee implemented the Child Care Red Tape Reduction Act (effective July 17) streamlining childcare-facility licensing statewide, and as advocates highlighted that more than 300,000 Tennessee children under age 5 need childcare and Nashville meets only 56% of that need — issues Ogles's campaign did not address publicly.

child_hunger.details: Tennessee Lookout reported (July 17) that at an agricultural forum for TN-5 candidates, Ogles billed himself as someone 'willing to buck leadership' and identified China as the 'greatest threat' to American food security, arguing the U.S. needs to be less dependent on China as a crop buyer — a food-security framing centered on trade policy, not on SNAP, school meals, or child nutrition programs. No statements from Ogles on SNAP cuts, Summer EBT, or child hunger were found during the study window, even as roughly 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and Civil Eats (July 16) reported on Tennessee SNAP recipients' struggles with new work requirements. Ogles did not respond to Tennessee Lookout's request for comment on district priorities.

parental_support.summary: Ogles's dominant news this week was his introduction of the 'Anchors Away Act,' which would restrict pregnant noncitizens' entry to the U.S. to prevent birthright citizenship for their children — a child/family-adjacent immigration measure — but he made no statements on paid leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare affordability.
parental_support.details: Ogles introduced the Anchors Away Act following a Supreme Court ruling on birthright citizenship, according to the Lake County Banner (July 16) and Newsmax (July 15-16) coverage. The bill would amend the Immigration and Nationality Act and would make certain pregnant nonimmigrant foreign nationals inadmissible if their primary purpose for entering the country is to obtain citizenship for a child through birth on American soil. Ogles said: 'Today, the Supreme Court cheapened the most valuable thing on planet Earth: U.S. citizenship... I refuse to let these anchor babies colonize our country. Save our sovereignty. Anchors away!' While this bill directly concerns childbirth and citizenship for children, it is an immigration-enforcement measure rather than a domestic family-economic policy; no statements from Ogles on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare affordability were found this week. Separately, Ogles continued to tout his endorsement from President Trump amid a competitive primary against Charlie Hatcher, with Punchbowl News (July 17) reporting a pro-clean-energy PAC has spent nearly $700,000 opposing him and that Ogles has been slow to fundraise and has aired almost no TV ads.

name: Charlie Hatcher
bio: Endorsed by former Gov. Bill Haslam and former Sen. Bob Corker. Considered the strongest Republican challenger to Ogles. $546K in FEC receipts with $214K cash on hand (Q1 2026).

early_childhood_ed.summary: In a July 17 Tennessee Lookout candidate questionnaire, Hatcher listed 'universal child care' among 'family first initiatives' he supports as part of his affordability agenda for TN-5, though he did not detail specific pre-K, Head Start, or licensing proposals.
early_childhood_ed.details: Asked by Tennessee Lookout to identify the three most pressing issues for TN-5 constituents, Hatcher named 'Affordability, Environmental Justice, and Healthcare Justice,' and under affordability said: 'There are also measures such as universal child care and other family first initiatives that will create space in our families' wallets,' alongside proposals to raise the minimum wage, cap credit card interest, and strengthen consumer protections against predatory lending. This is Hatcher's only documented statement on childcare/early education policy during the window; his other public appearances this week — including a July 9 talk at the Franklin Noon Rotary Club (reported July 16 by the Williamson Herald) held at High Hopes Preschool and Pediatric Therapy in Franklin — focused on his family's dairy-farming history rather than childcare policy specifics. Hatcher's campaign this week also received the high-profile endorsement of former Gov. Bill Haslam (Tennessean, Williamson Herald, both July 16-17), adding to prior endorsements from former U.S. Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue and former Rep. Zach Wamp.

child_hunger.summary: Hatcher, the former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner, framed food security as a national-security and agricultural-trade issue in his July 17 Tennessee Lookout platform statement, but made no specific comments on SNAP, school meals, or child nutrition programs this week.
child_hunger.details: In his Tennessee Lookout candidate response, Hatcher wrote that 'Food security is national security, and this is my wheelhouse,' arguing the U.S. 'must support and protect American farmers from foreign adversaries, unfair trade practices, and policies that threaten our ability to produce our own food' and warning that 'a country that cannot feed itself cannot remain secure or independent.' This framing emphasizes agricultural production and trade policy rather than domestic nutrition-assistance programs like SNAP or school meals; Hatcher did not comment on the roughly 100,000 Tennesseans who lost SNAP benefits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. His campaign messaging elsewhere this week, including endorsement announcements from Gov. Haslam and Secretary Perdue, emphasized his decade-long agricultural credentials but similarly did not address child nutrition assistance programs.

parental_support.summary: Hatcher's July 17 Tennessee Lookout statement grouped 'universal child care' with broader 'family first initiatives' meant to ease household budgets, alongside minimum-wage increases and consumer-lending protections, but he offered no specific paid-leave or Child Tax Credit proposals this week.
parental_support.details: Hatcher's platform statement to Tennessee Lookout emphasized affordability for families: 'For affordability, I plan to support and craft legislation that raises the minimum wage to lead to living wages, support the bipartisan legislation to cap credit card interest, and strengthen consumer financial protections to prevent predatory lending and payday loans. There are also measures such as universal child care and other family first initiatives that will create space in our families' wallets.' No further detail on paid family leave or the Child Tax Credit was found. Hatcher, a self-described 'author, husband, father and grandfather,' also spoke at length about his family history at the July 9 Franklin Noon Rotary luncheon (reported July 16), sharing multi-generational stories about the Hatcher family and Hatcher Family Dairy, though that appearance centered on personal biography rather than family policy. His campaign gained momentum this week with the endorsement of former Gov. Bill Haslam, who praised Hatcher's 'commonsense approach to getting back to the basics of what made our country great.'

bio: DCCC top target. Has raised $1.81M total ($978K cash on hand, Q1 2026). Leads Republican candidates in fundraising. Centrist Democrat with crossover appeal in a swing district.
